Reporting verification progress as a single aggregate percentage obscures critical engineering vulnerabilities. A safety case cannot rely on a summary metric stating that a machine survived ninety-eight percent of five thousand fault trials if all five thousand injections were conducted at room temperature on a quiescent memory bus. Coverage must instead be reported across separate operational dimensions, including functional safety requirements, physical envelope boundaries, physical and logical injection sites, timing tails, hardware build revisions, and multi-fault combinations. For a flow regulator, boundary coverage tracks whether faults were injected at maximum fluid viscosity, minimum back-pressure, and maximum pump ripple. Timing tail coverage isolates injections targeting the $P_{99}$ scheduling latency of the nervous system and peak direct memory access utilization. A machine achieves acceptable verification not when an average coverage index exceeds an arbitrary threshold, but when the minimum coverage across every individual dimension satisfies the requirements of the safety case.[^fn-std-iso26262-fault-injection]

Interpreting repeated trials requires distinguishing between deterministic execution and stochastic sampling. Repeating the exact same deterministic fault script five hundred times on a digital test bench yields no more information than running it once. If initial conditions, processor register states, clock dividers, and input sequences are fixed, identical deterministic software executes the identical branch sequence every time. Repetition adds evidentiary value only when sampling physical and computational distributions that exhibit stochastic variance. In a physical flow loop, repeated trials sample turbulent velocity fluctuations, asynchronous interrupt arrivals, bus arbitration contention, and phase jitter between the high-frequency sensor clock and the policy inference cycle. In these stochastic regimes, repetition measures the spread and tail of the response-time distribution rather than re-confirming a deterministic path.

When a stochastic trial runs $n$ consecutive times without a single safety violation, the count of zero-failure trials bounds the maximum underlying failure probability $p$ for that specific test distribution.[^fn-math-clopper-pearson] If each trial has an independent failure probability $p$, the probability of observing zero failures across $n$ independent trials is $(1 - p)^n$. To establish that the failure probability is bounded above by $p$ at a statistical confidence level of $1 - \alpha$, the probability of observing an all-pass outcome by chance from an unsafe system must not exceed $\alpha$, yielding $(1 - p)^n \le \alpha$. Taking the natural logarithm of both sides gives $n \ln(1 - p) \le \ln(\alpha)$. For rare failure rates where $p \ll 1$, the first-order Taylor expansion $\ln(1 - p) \approx -p$ provides the standard engineering approximation $n \ge -\ln(\alpha) / p$. For an exact calculation to bound the failure probability below one percent ($p \le 0.01$) at ninety-five percent confidence ($\alpha = 0.05$), the inequality is $(1 - 0.01)^n \le 0.05$. Taking logarithms produces $n \ge \ln(0.05) / \ln(0.99) \approx -2.9957 / -0.01005 \approx 298.07$, which requires exactly $299$ independent, zero-failure trials.

The statistical validity of this one-sided binomial bound depends entirely on two physical assumptions, namely trial independence and operational representativeness. Independence requires that the outcome of trial $k$ has no effect on trial $k+1$. If repeated fault injections cause resistive heating in a valve solenoid coil, increasing coil resistance and slowing valve actuation across successive tests, the trials are coupled by a hidden thermal state, and the binomial formula is invalid. Representativeness requires that the test conditions accurately reflect the true operational environment. Running 299 successful fault injections under steady, laminar flow at $20^\circ\text{C}$ proves that the failure probability is below one percent at ninety-five percent confidence only for laminar flow at $20^\circ\text{C}$. It provides zero empirical or mathematical basis for claiming safety during turbulent flow, severe cavitation, or cold-start operations at $-10^\circ\text{C}$.

::: {.callout-math title="Hardware Fault Injection Coverage and Mean Time Between Unmitigated Faults (MTBUF)"}
*Scenario:* An autonomous physical AI system operates with a cumulative raw hardware component failure rate $\lambda_{\text{raw}}$ across its perception sensors, communication transceivers, microcontrollers, and inverter gate drivers. We calculate the diagnostic coverage $C_{\text{diag}}$ that Hardware-in-the-Loop (HIL) fault injection must empirically prove to achieve a target Mean Time Between Unmitigated Faults ($\text{MTBUF}$) of $10^7\text{ hours}$ (equivalent to an unmitigated failure rate $\lambda_{\text{unmitigated}} \le 10^{-7}\text{ h}^{-1} = 100\text{ FIT}$), and derive the required number of zero-failure HIL test trials $N_{\text{trials}}$.

**System Failure Rate & Unmitigated Failure Relation:**
$$\lambda_{\text{unmitigated}} = \lambda_{\text{raw}} \cdot (1 - C_{\text{diag}}) \implies \text{MTBUF} = \frac{1}{\lambda_{\text{unmitigated}}} = \frac{1}{\lambda_{\text{raw}} (1 - C_{\text{diag}})}$$
Solving for required diagnostic coverage:
$$C_{\text{diag}} \ge 1 - \frac{\lambda_{\text{unmitigated}}}{\lambda_{\text{raw}}} = 1 - \frac{1}{\text{MTBUF} \cdot \lambda_{\text{raw}}}$$

**1. Cumulative Raw Hardware Failure Rate:**
Suppose an embedded computing and actuation stack incorporates:

- 4 CMOS cameras + 2 LiDAR modules: $\lambda_{\text{sensors}} = 6 \times 250\text{ FIT} = 1,500\text{ FIT}$
- 2 Dual-Brain SoCs (Linux MPUs + Safety MCUs): $\lambda_{\text{compute}} = 2 \times 500\text{ FIT} = 1,000\text{ FIT}$
- CAN/Ethernet Transceivers + Power Distribution PMICs: $\lambda_{\text{bus/power}} = 2,500\text{ FIT}$
- 6 Inverter Power Stages and Gate Drivers: $\lambda_{\text{inverters}} = 6 \times 800\text{ FIT} = 4,800\text{ FIT}$
- Total raw hardware failure rate:
$$\begin{aligned}
\lambda_{\text{raw}} &= 1,500 + 1,000 + 2,500 + 4,800 = 9,800\text{ FIT} \\
&= 9.8 \times 10^{-6}\text{ faults/h} \quad (\approx 1\text{ raw fault per } 102,000\text{ hours})
\end{aligned}$$

**2. Required Diagnostic Coverage Calculation:**
To guarantee an unmitigated catastrophic failure rate $\lambda_{\text{unmitigated}} \le 10^{-7}\text{ h}^{-1}$ ($\text{MTBUF} \ge 10^7\text{ hours}$):
$$C_{\text{diag}} \ge 1 - \frac{10^{-7}\text{ h}^{-1}}{9.8 \times 10^{-6}\text{ h}^{-1}} = 1 - 0.0102 = 0.9898 \implies C_{\text{diag}} \ge 99.0\%$$

**3. Required Statistical Zero-Failure HIL Test Count:**
Using the exact Clopper-Pearson binomial tail bound at $95\%$ confidence ($\alpha = 0.05$):
$$\begin{aligned}
(1 - p_{\text{unmitigated}})^N &\le \alpha \implies N_{\text{trials}} \ge \frac{\ln(\alpha)}{\ln(C_{\text{diag}})} \\
&= \frac{\ln(0.05)}{\ln(0.990)} \approx \frac{-2.9957}{-0.01005} \approx 298.1 \implies 299\text{ trials}
\end{aligned}$$
If safety integrity escalates to ASIL D ($C_{\text{diag}} \ge 99.9\%$, $p_{\text{unmitigated}} \le 0.001$):
$$N_{\text{trials}} \ge \frac{-\ln(0.05)}{1 - 0.999} = \frac{2.9957}{0.001} \approx 2,996\text{ consecutive zero-failure HIL injection trials}$$

*Archetype coverage comparison:*

- *Mobile System (Autonomous Ground Transport):* Total raw rate $\lambda_{\text{raw}} = 1.2 \times 10^{-5}\text{ h}^{-1}$; targeting ASIL D unmitigated rate ($10^{-8}\text{ h}^{-1}$) requires $C_{\text{diag}} \ge 99.92\%$, demanding $3,745$ zero-failure HIL brake/steer brownout injections.
- *Manipulator (6-DoF Articulated Arm):* Raw joint inverter rate $\lambda_{\text{raw}} = 6.0 \times 10^{-6}\text{ h}^{-1}$; targeting SIL 3 ($10^{-7}\text{ h}^{-1}$) requires $C_{\text{diag}} \ge 98.33\%$, requiring $179$ zero-failure joint-stall brake clamp trials.
- *Process System (High-Pressure Flow Regulator):* Raw transducer/valve rate $\lambda_{\text{raw}} = 8.5 \times 10^{-6}\text{ h}^{-1}$; targeting $10^{-7}\text{ h}^{-1}$ requires $C_{\text{diag}} \ge 98.82\%$, demanding $253$ zero-failure cavitation/stale-pressure injection trials.
:::

When target reliability requirements scale from advisory levels to life-critical integrity levels, the sample size required by binomial and exponential tail bounds becomes physically impossible to achieve through black-box operational exposure alone. This fundamental limitation—formalized by Butler and Finelli [@butler1993infeasibility] as the **Butler & Finelli Infeasibility Bound**—dictates that certifying ultra-high cyber-physical reliability (e.g., $10^{-9}$ catastrophic failures per hour) through unperturbed operational exposure alone is physically impossible due to astronomical time requirements (e.g., $>3.0 \times 10^9\text{ hours}$ of continuous zero-failure testing), mathematically necessitating deterministic fault injection, layered runtime invariant enforcement, and formal architectural partitioning.

As quantified in @tbl-15-statistical-testing-bounds, certifying an avionics DAL A or ISO 26262 ASIL D catastrophic failure rate of $10^{-9}\text{ h}^{-1}$ at $95\%$ confidence requires over $3.0 \times 10^9\text{ hours}$ (more than 342,000 years) of continuous, zero-failure physical operation. Even a distributed fleet of 100 dedicated test vehicles operating continuously 24 hours a day would require over 3,400 years to establish this statistical claim. Consequently, physical AI systems cannot be validated solely by accumulating millions of unperturbed operational fleet miles; safety assurance must instead be established through deterministic fault injection, layered runtime invariant enforcement, and formal architectural partitioning.

|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|

| **Industrial Automation (SIL 2 / PL d)**<br>*(IEC 61508 / ISO 13849)*      | $10^{-6}\text{ h}^{-1}$<br>*(1 failure / $10^6\text{ h}$)* | $p \approx 2.78 \times 10^{-12}$                             | $3.0 \times 10^6\text{ h}$              | $3.0 \times 10^6\text{ h}$<br>*(342 years continuous)*     | $3.4\text{ years}$<br>*(at 24/7 continuous operation)* | **Hybrid Verification:** Statistical sampling paired with accelerated fault injection and HIL parameter stress sweeps.                                                                 |
| **Automotive Safety (ASIL D / SIL 3)**<br>*(ISO 26262 / IEC 61508)*        | $10^{-8}\text{ h}^{-1}$<br>*(10 FIT / $10^8\text{ h}$)*    | $p \approx 2.78 \times 10^{-14}$                             | $3.0 \times 10^8\text{ h}$              | $3.0 \times 10^8\text{ h}$<br>*(34,200 years continuous)*  | $342\text{ years}$<br>*(100 vehicles 24/7)*            | **Architectural Containment Mandatory:** Formal invariant synthesis, hardware interlocks, and systematic fault injection; fleet testing cannot prove safety.                           |
| **Life-Critical Avionics (DAL A / SIL 4)**<br>*(DO-178C / FAA AC 20-115D)* | $10^{-9}\text{ h}^{-1}$<br>*(1 failure / $10^9\text{ h}$)* | $p \approx 2.78 \times 10^{-15}$                             | $3.0 \times 10^9\text{ h}$              | $3.0 \times 10^9\text{ h}$<br>*(342,465 years continuous)* | $3,425\text{ years}$<br>*(100 units 24/7 continuous)*  | **Mathematical Impossibility of Black-Box Test:** Safety *cannot* be established by fleet exposure. Provenance, formal methods, and isolated intervention are mathematically required. |
: **Statistical Confidence vs. Physical Testing Exposure Bounds across Safety Integrity Levels.** Quantification of required zero-failure test exposure ($T = -\ln(1-C)/\lambda$ at $C=0.95$ confidence) and physical operational fleet hours per Butler & Finelli [@butler1993infeasibility], demonstrating the mathematical infeasibility of certifying life-critical cyber-physical systems through black-box operational burn-in alone. {#tbl-15-statistical-testing-bounds}

A defensible safety case requires that untested operational envelopes, unobservable test results, and unsupported probability claims be presented with the exact same visual and structural prominence as successful verifications. Hiding an untested envelope boundary or an unverified hardware permutation in an appendix manufactures a false impression of completeness. The fault record must explicitly list every parameter combination where fault injection was omitted due to test bench limitations, sensor bandwidth constraints, or destructive hardware limits. Documenting what was never tested prevents unverified operational zones from silently masquerading as verified safety margins when the record is transferred to the safety case in @sec-release. Furthermore, every isolated entry in the record documents the response of the machine to a single, localized disturbance. In physical operation, however, disturbances rarely occur in strict isolation, and verifying how a machine responds to an individual fault leaves open the question of how it behaves when multiple nominal disturbances strike the system at the same time.
<!-- END -->

## Systems Stress-Tests {#sec-verification-15-8}

<!-- SECTION 15.8 -->
<!-- claim: A fault that passes individually and fails in combination. -->
<!-- covers: Derive compound tests from shared resources, common causes, detector dependencies, and budgets that add across handoffs rather than enumerating every fault pair. -->
<!-- covers: Show a flow regulator in which 120 ms of observation delay and 150 ms of planning delay each satisfy a local 200 ms limit but together exceed a 250 ms end-to-end physical margin. -->
<!-- covers: Test whether bus saturation simultaneously delays observations, plans, enforcement telemetry, and the evidence logger. -->
<!-- covers: Include a case in which one fault disables the detector needed to contain the second fault. -->
<!-- covers: Treat an unobservable outcome as an invalid test and an instrumentation defect, never as evidence that the machine held. -->
<!-- covers: Record the interaction responsible for failure so Chapter 16 can condition or refuse release on that shared cause. -->
<!-- DERIVE: compound fault priorities from common causes, shared resources, and composed margins rather than selecting combinations arbitrarily -->

<!-- BEGIN -->
A machine that passes every isolated fault injection test can fail when two nominal disturbances occur at the same time. If a system possesses $N$ cataloged failure modes, testing every arbitrary pair requires $\mathcal{O}(N^2)$ injection trials, and higher-order combinations expand exponentially. Exhaustive combinatorial injection is physically intractable, and unguided random sampling wastes testing resources on independent components that share no physical or logical connection. Systems stress-testing avoids combinatorial explosion by deriving compound fault vectors directly from shared physical resources, common electrical paths, cascading detector dependencies, and latency budgets that accumulate across handoffs. The following four analytical stress-tests evaluate machines where individually compliant subsystems combine into catastrophic physical failures:

### Stress-Test 1: Compound Latency Accumulation across Distributed Handoffs {.unnumbered}

*The scenario.* An industrial liquid-propellant flow regulator ($P_{\text{inlet}} = 12.0\text{ MPa}$, nominal flow $15.0\text{ kg/s}$) requires flow transients to be arrested within an end-to-end deadline of $250.0\text{ ms}$ to prevent chamber rupture at $14.5\text{ MPa}$. Execution is distributed across three nodes on a shared $10\text{ Mbps}$ CAN bus: an optical densitometer (ingest budget $80.0\text{ ms}$), a GPU inference node (execution budget $120.0\text{ ms}$), and a valve actuator node (budget $40.0\text{ ms}$). In standalone tests, sensor delay ($75.0\text{ ms}$), inference delay ($115.0\text{ ms}$), and valve delay ($38.0\text{ ms}$) all pass local watchdog limits.

*The systems dilemma.* When an upstream cavitation surge occurs, sensor, planner, and actuator simultaneously experience their worst-case individually compliant delays, while unthrottled diagnostic logging adds $45.0\text{ ms}$ of bus queuing. Total cumulative latency reaches $75.0\text{ ms} + 115.0\text{ ms} + 38.0\text{ ms} + 45.0\text{ ms} = 273.0\text{ ms}$, exceeding the $250.0\text{ ms}$ physical vessel limit by $23.0\text{ ms}$ and bursting the vessel while every local watchdog reports nominal health.

*The systems verdict: Additive Timing Composition Law.* Local watchdog timers are mathematically incapable of guaranteeing end-to-end physical safety when handoff delays accumulate. Verification must enforce distributed end-to-end deadline tracking rather than isolated component timeouts.

### Stress-Test 2: Shared Bus Saturation and Control Loop Starvation {.unnumbered}

*The scenario.* An autonomous platform coordinates sensing, neural inference, safety reflexes, and evidence logging across a single shared field bus. An unthrottled diagnostic flight-recorder memory dump pushes bus utilization to $98\%$.

*The systems dilemma.* Bus contention does not produce an isolated delay in a single subsystem; it simultaneously delays raw sensor packets to the planner, setpoints to valve actuators, heartbeats to the safety enforcer, and crash logs to the evidence ledger. The simultaneous loss of actuator commands and enforcement telemetry starves the safety loop, preventing the monitor from detecting an actuator freeze.

*The systems verdict: Shared Interconnect Contention Invariant.* Common communication media couple previously independent subsystems during transients. Critical safety heartbeats and actuator telemetry must reside on isolated physical channels or hardware-prioritized time-triggered slots.

### Stress-Test 3: Asymmetric Detector Dependency under Supply Transients {.unnumbered}

*The scenario.* A power supply ripple causes an optical flow meter to experience a digital register freeze, latching output telemetry at a steady nominal $4.2\text{ kg/s}$. Concurrently, a mechanical valve blockage restricts physical flow to $0.8\text{ kg/s}$.

*The systems dilemma.* Because the latched value ($4.2\text{ kg/s}$) falls within nominal bounds and generates no framing errors, the anomaly detector never flags a fault. The neural planner reads nominal flow and issues no corrective command, preventing the safety enforcer from opening the auxiliary relief line. Testing the blockage alone or the sensor freeze alone passes; only the compound test exposes the disabled detector.

*The systems verdict: Asymmetric Detector Dependency Law.* A primary electrical fault can disable the exact sensory detector required to contain a secondary mechanical failure. Verification must audit the causal graph to ensure safety monitors rely on physically independent, cross-modal transducers.

### Stress-Test 4: Unobservable Trial Outcomes under Diagnostic Reset {.unnumbered}

*The scenario.* During an aggressive multi-fault injection test on high-speed motion hardware, bus contention causes the testbench data logger to drop packets, and an emergency watchdog reset wipes volatile diagnostic trace RAM.

*The systems dilemma.* Because the recording apparatus failed, the physical trajectory, peak reaction forces, and timing margins throughout the transient cannot be reconstructed. The test team attempts to score the trial as a "pass" because the physical machine did not strike mechanical stops.

*The systems verdict: Unobservable Trial Invalidation Law.* An unobservable outcome is an invalid test and an instrumentation defect, never evidence that the machine survived. If the testbed cannot deterministically measure state throughout a fault transient, the run yields zero evidentiary value.
<!-- END -->

## Summary {#sec-verification-15-9}

<!-- SECTION 15.9 -->
<!-- claim: Chapter 13 receives evidence rather than confidence. -->
<!-- covers: Distill the distinction between a successful demonstration and evidence tied to a bounded claim. -->
<!-- covers: Restate that the operating envelope determines which violations are meaningful and reproducible. -->
<!-- covers: Carry forward the traceability from each prior property through its injected fault, detector, response, and measured outcome. -->
<!-- covers: State that every qualification mode leaves explicit evidentiary limits and that untested conditions remain open claims. -->
<!-- covers: Hand Chapter 16 a versioned fault record containing passes, failures, invalid tests, coverage gaps, and unsupported probability claims. -->

<!-- BEGIN -->
A demonstration shows that a machine can function under favorable circumstances, while verification generates structured evidence that a design claim holds when those circumstances fail. In an analytical example of an industrial flow regulator, allowing an observer to watch an automated control loop maintain line pressure at $4.0\text{ MPa}$ across three uninterrupted operating shifts proves only that the nominal trajectory did not encounter an unhandled disturbance. It does not establish what happens when a proportional relief valve jams at $15\%$ travel during a sudden pump surge, or whether the pressure transducer's degraded bandwidth violates the intervention deadline. A demonstration produces confidence, which is psychological and decays with the first unexpected physical transient. Verification produces evidence, which is an auditable record of bounded claims tested against deliberate physical and computational stress. Downstream systems and safety cases receive this concrete evidence rather than subjective confidence.

The operating envelope defines the physical boundary within which safety claims are made, evaluated, and reproduced. Outside this envelope, physical dynamics deviate from the models used during design, turning test results into uninterpretable noise. Inside it, every parameter boundary corresponds to a specific physical constraint, such as an inlet fluid velocity ceiling of $6.0\text{ m/s}$ or an ambient temperature limit of $65.0^\circ\text{C}$. When a stress-test injects an upstream pressure surge of $1.5\text{ MPa/s}$ into the regulator, the test is meaningful only because the design explicitly claimed stability across pressure derivatives up to $2.0\text{ MPa/s}$. If a test exposes a pressure overshoot exceeding the $5.0\text{ MPa}$ structural vessel limit while operating within this boundary, the failure is reproducible and falsifies the design claim. If an identical pressure overshoot occurs only after the fluid velocity exceeds $9.0\text{ m/s}$, the failure indicates that the test apparatus breached the operating envelope, measuring physics that the controller was never budgeted to reject.

Verification derives its structure from the properties established across the preceding design stages. Every contract stated in the pipeline becomes an explicit fault waiting to be injected into the assembled machine. For the flow regulator, the design claims from earlier chapters dictate a strict chain of traceability. A sensor calibration claim from the perception pipeline becomes an injected drift fault of $0.2\text{ MPa}$, testing whether the diagnostic estimator detects the discrepancy before flow estimation errors propagate to the policy. A policy latency claim of $115\text{ ms}$ at $P_{99}$ becomes an injected inference jitter fault, verifying that the nervous system detects the schedule overrun and executes an immediate fallback trajectory. An actuator authority claim becomes an injected valve slew saturation fault, confirming that the mechanical intervention mechanism isolates the line within the $250\text{ ms}$ physical vessel budget. Each verification vector links five distinct elements in an unbroken chain, connecting the original design property, the injected disturbance, the runtime detector, the nervous system response, and the final measured physical state.

Every qualification mode operates under explicit evidentiary limits. Hardware-in-the-loop simulation permits dense sampling of rare boundary crossings, running thousands of synthetic cavitation transients without wearing out physical seals, but it remains blind to unmodeled hydrodynamic turbulence and bus transceiver heating. Physical dynamometer testing captures true thermal dissipation, electromagnetic interference, and mechanical backlash, but it cannot safely execute destructive overpressurization tests to failure across hundreds of consecutive runs. Treating a simulated pass as proof of physical compliance confuses the fidelity of a model with physical reality. Conversely, treating a physical test under a single ambient condition as a universal guarantee ignores environmental coupling. Any operating condition, input distribution, or hardware degradation state that has not been subjected to deliberate fault injection remains an open claim rather than an established property.

::: {.callout-takeaways}
- **Demonstrations Build Psychological Confidence; Verification Generates Auditable Evidence:** Watching a machine run without failure proves only that nominal conditions held. Verification requires deliberate physical fault injection across boundary envelopes to prove that safety invariants hold when subsystems fail.
- **Local Watchdogs Cannot Prevent Additive Timing Failure:** If sensor ($75\text{ ms}$), GPU inference ($115\text{ ms}$), valve actuator ($38\text{ ms}$), and diagnostic logging ($45\text{ ms}$) all operate within local limits, their sum ($273\text{ ms}$) breaches the physical vessel limit ($250\text{ ms}$). Safety verification must track end-to-end distributed deadline accumulation.
- **Compound Fault Vectors Must Trace Shared Physical Resources:** Testing single faults in isolation misses catastrophic interactions. Electrical voltage ripples can freeze digital register outputs at nominal values, disabling the exact software anomaly detector needed to catch a concurrent mechanical valve jam.
- **Unobservable Test Outcomes Yield Zero Evidentiary Value:** If testbed data loggers drop packets or watchdog resets wipe diagnostic trace RAM during a fault transient, the run is an invalid test, never evidence that the machine survived the fault.
- **The Versioned Fault Record is the Sole Prerequisite for Release:** The output of verification is an immutable fault record cataloging verified passes, hard failures, invalid runs, and explicit coverage gaps handed directly to the release assurance safety case.
:::

The output of this verification process is a versioned fault record delivered directly to the safety case assembled in @sec-release. This record documents the outcome of every injected vector without aggregation or statistical smoothing. It details the verified passes where measured bounds held with quantifiable margins, the hard failures where detection or intervention deadlines were missed, and the invalid tests where testbed artifacts or envelope violations corrupted the data. It highlights the remaining coverage gaps where test vectors could not be safely or physically executed, and it explicitly flags unsupported probability claims where rare-event tail distributions were estimated without sufficient sample depth. @sec-release builds the formal assurance argument that justifies operating the machine, converting the fault record into bounded claims for release. When those physical evidence bounds confront the open-world distribution shift and rare, unmodeled hazards of deployment, @sec-frontier synthesizes the overarching epistemic boundary of physical AI, establishing how runtime systems enforce safety even when verification reaches its fundamental limits.
<!-- END -->

[^fn-std-stpa-leveson]: Leveson (2011) demonstrated via STAMP/STPA that in complex cyber-physical architectures, catastrophic hazards often arise not from individual component failures, but from unsafe, unhandled interactions among correctly operating subsystems whose local control assumptions conflict.

[^fn-hw-seu-bitflip]: On safety microcontrollers (ARM Cortex-R5F, Infineon AURIX), dedicated fault injection registers and BIST controllers flip SRAM bits to verify that ECC SECDED triggers an immediate Non-Maskable Interrupt (NMI) before corrupted coordinates reach actuator PWM registers.

[^fn-inc-apollo-1202]: During Apollo 11's lunar descent, asynchronous radar pulses flooded the AGC with unbudgeted interrupts, stealing $15\%$ of CPU cycles and triggering 1202 alarms. The lander survived because priority-scheduled core memory dropped low-priority display tasks to maintain thruster cycles.

[^fn-inc-toyota-ua]: Forensic analysis in *Bookout v. Toyota* (2013) revealed unbounded stack growth and a fatal architectural flaw: the hardware watchdog timer was refreshed by an asynchronous OS monitor task that continued executing after the primary throttle control task had died.

[^fn-std-iso26262-fault-injection]: ANSI/UL 4600 mandates goal-based safety cases linking claims to traceable evidence rather than raw operational hours. Similarly, ISO 26262-5 mandates hardware fault injection to verify ASIL D diagnostic coverage (Single-Point Fault Metric $\ge 99\%$, Latent Fault Metric $\ge 90\%$).

[^fn-math-clopper-pearson]: For zero-failure testing, standard Wald confidence intervals degenerate to zero width. The exact Clopper-Pearson interval yields $p_{\text{upper}} = 1 - \alpha^{1/n}$, preventing asymptotic Gaussian approximations from understating catastrophic risk in rare-event tail distributions.
